title: Heard in the world
hook: from Jakarta to Dakar, the same Arabic is recited every day

segments.voice: Yesterday, khatm: the whole book, sealed, and begun again. Your line was the whole book, once. Day three hundred twenty-nine, the end of a week.

Dawn is a moving line. Right now it's reaching a new strip of the earth, and somewhere in that strip, someone is standing to pray and reciting al-Fatiha. An hour from now the line will have moved west, and someone else will be saying the same seven verses in the same Arabic. Follow the dawn around the planet and you'll hear the Qur'an recited in every time zone.
screen: `DAWN IS A MOVING LINE.` → `THE SAME SEVEN VERSES.` → `EVERY TIME ZONE.`

segments.voice: Demographers put the number of Muslims near two billion, and most of them are not Arabs. Indonesia has more Muslims than any other country. Muslims speak a great many languages at home, from Javanese to Hausa to Bosnian to English. Yet the five daily prayers are said in the same Arabic: a child in Jakarta and a grandmother in Dakar recite the Fatiha in the same sounds. The Qur'an names that variety as a sign. In Pickthall's words: "And of His signs is the creation of the heavens and the earth, and the difference of your languages and colours." Different tongues, one recitation. And each place has its own sound. Egypt's twentieth-century reciters, heard on the radio, carried a long, melodic style far beyond Egypt. Imams in the Gulf are often heard in a plainer, flowing style. In Morocco you may hear the reading of Warsh, met last week. Indonesia and Malaysia hold national recitation competitions, where young men and women recite before large crowds. Turkish reciters have their own ornamented tradition. Same words, different voices, and this week showed why that holds together. The hafiz carries it by heart. The sajdah verses bring a room to the floor. The longest and the shortest, al-Baqarah and al-Kawthar. Iltifat, who is speaking: We, I, He, and say. The mushaf, handled with care. Khatm, the whole book. And now the whole world, reciting it.
screen: `NEAR TWO BILLION, MOSTLY NOT ARABS` · `ONE ARABIC, FIVE TIMES A DAY` · `YOUR LANGUAGES AND COLORS: A SIGN` · `EACH PLACE HAS ITS OWN SOUND`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and picture that line of dawn moving across the earth, and along it, voice after voice, in the same words; if you recite, let your voice be one of them. Another time, play a recitation from somewhere you've never been: an Indonesian competition, a West African reciter in Warsh, an Egyptian master from the radio years.
Al-'Alamin. The worlds — as in rabb al-'alamin, Lord of the worlds, the same Arabic recited from Jakarta to Dakar. Today's word.
Your line: the same words everywhere. The difference of your languages is a sign. And that closes the week.

howItsDone: The daily prayers are recited in Arabic whatever language a Muslim speaks at home, and many regions have their own well-known reciters and styles of recitation.
